overview: White fianchettoes the queen's bishop on b2 and keeps the centre flexible, usually answering ...d5 or ...e6 with Bb2, e3 and a later d4 or c4. Black can build a classical centre with ...d5 and ...e6 or fianchetto with ...g6. The game is a slow manoeuvring fight where White pressures e5 and the long diagonal rather than occupying the centre early.

white_ideas.idea: Bb2 on the long diagonal, e3, g3/Bg2 or d3, then c4 or d4 at the right moment
Pressure e5 and control the centre with pieces rather than pawns

black_ideas.idea: Claim the centre with ...d5, ...e6 and ...c5 or ...Bb4
Mirror the fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, or hit the b2 bishop with ...b6

typical_structures.structure: White queenside fianchetto against a ...d5/...e6 centre, the pawn on d4 delayed

character.notes: Slow flank opening, no early forcing play; steady manoeuvring and few ways to lose quickly, but not especially hard to break down either.

soundness.notes: Fully respectable; Larsen and Nimzowitsch played it at top level.

structure.notes: Centre left undecided for many moves; White decides between d4 and c4 later.

approach.notes: b3/Bb2/e3 can be set up against most replies, though it is usually filed as a Reti-type flank opening rather than a pure system.

level.notes: Clear piece placement, modest theory, but the right moment for d4 or c4 takes judgement.

character.reason: Quiet flank play that is neither especially hard to crack nor tactical.

soundness.reason: A respectable line used by strong players.

structure.reason: The centre stays undecided, as in the English and Reti.

approach.reason: Played at all levels, though the b3/Bb2 set-up could be called a system.

level.reason: Simple piece placement but timing of the central break takes judgement.

plans.reason: Bb2 on the long diagonal with the centre contested by pieces.
